[PATH:empirical] Systematic evaluation of LLMs on novel, multi-step planning benchmarks (e.g., new variants of the 'Blocks World' or 'Sokoban' tasks requiring generalization to unseen state spaces) — Directly tests the hypothesis that LLMs have fundamental planning deficits by measuring performance on tasks designed to require genuine planning rather than pattern matching from training data. Consistent failure across diverse, novel planning benchmarks would support the hypothesis, while success would challenge it.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of transformer expressiveness limits (e.g., circuit complexity bounds, TC0 vs. P/poly separations) applied to reasoning tasks required for AGI — Investigates whether transformer architectures (the backbone of current LLMs) are fundamentally incapable of certain types of reasoning (e.g., iterative depth-first search, composition of long reasoning chains) that are plausibly necessary for AGI. Formal proofs of such limitations would confirm the hypothesis, while results showing equivalence to universal computation would refute it.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of published results on LLM 'reasoning' (e.g., chain-of-thought, self-consistency, tool use) from top AI conferences (NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR) over the past 5 years, focusing on failure modes in out-of-distribution, compositional, or causal reasoning tasks — Aggregates existing empirical evidence to assess whether reported reasoning capabilities are robust or brittle. A systematic literature review revealing that LLMs consistently fail on non-trivial, out-of-distribution reasoning tasks (e.g., GSM8K variants, MATH, or causal inference benchmarks) would strengthen the hypothesis, whereas evidence of broad, reliable generalization would weaken it.

[PATH:empirical] Empirical tracking of scaling laws for LLMs beyond current compute budgets (e.g., training models with 10^26 FLOPs or more) to see if emergent reasoning capabilities plateau or continue to improve linearly with scale — If scaling laws show diminishing returns or a ceiling on novel reasoning abilities, that would refute the hypothesis that scaling alone leads to AGI; continued linear or super-linear improvement in general problem-solving would support the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of computational requirements for AGI based on known cognitive architectures and information-theoretic bounds, e.g., comparing the functional complexity of human-level cognition to the representational capacity of current transformer models — A rigorous theoretical argument that current architectures lack necessary components (e.g., causal reasoning, long-term memory, or self-reflection) even at extreme scale would support the hypothesis that scaling will not lead to AGI; otherwise, it would be weakened.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of historical predictions and empirical results on AI capabilities from 2020-2024, focusing on whether scaling alone has produced unexpected general abilities (e.g., theory of mind, transfer learning) or has hit fundamental bottlenecks — Synthesizing existing evidence on the relationship between scale and emergent abilities can reveal patterns that confirm or refute the hypothesis, especially if prior scaling milestones have consistently failed to yield AGI-like generalization.
